title: Sharing Your Faith Without Fear
description: There’s nothing greater, nothing more significant we can share with others than the message of the gospel. And yet, if we’re honest, we often fail to speak about this good news to unbelievers God has put in our lives. We’re silent about the hope of eternal life because we’re worried about what others will think. In this sermon based on Acts 18:1–17, David Platt encourages us to share the gospel without fear. Even though opposition is inevitable, God’s power and His mission are unstoppable. Explore more content from  Radical .

fetched_title: Sharing Your Faith Without Fear - David Platt Messages

title: Behold His Faithfulness
description: Keeping your word seems to matter very little in our culture. Politicians unashamedly break promises, the covenant of marriage is trivialized, and, if we’re honest, each of us is tempted in a thousand little ways to distort the truth in our own lives. But, according to Psalm 98, we serve a God who is always faithful. In this sermon, David Platt encourages us to behold the God who shows steadfast love to His undeserving people. Such faithfulness should continually elicit our praise.  Explore more content from  Radical .

fetched_title: Behold His Faithfulness - David Platt Messages

title: Behold His Grace
description: Many followers of Christ cringe when the topic of giving comes up. Even when we do give, we’re often motivated more by guilt than gratitude. But this is not how Scripture motivates us to give. In this sermon on Psalm 86, David Platt points us to several biblical motives for our giving. We give in response to God’s infinite grace so that others might see His glory. Explore more content from  Radical .

fetched_title: Behold His Grace - David Platt Messages

title: Behold His Love
description: Sadly, some professing Christians find very little joy in their relationship with God. Trusting and obeying Him is a duty, not a delight. However, Psalm 63 reminds us that God’s great love ought to draw out deep affection from God’s people. In this sermon David Platt urges us to set aside lukewarm thoughts toward God and instead pursue Him as our all-consuming passion. Explore more content from  Radical .

fetched_title: Behold His Love - David Platt Messages

title: The Mercy of God in the Movement of the Peoples
description: The scale of the current refugee crisis is massive, and it can seem like events are spinning out of control. But what if God is using these tragedies to accomplish His global purposes? In this sermon on Acts 17:26–27, David Platt encourages us to view the movements of refugees around the world through the lens of God’s sovereignty and His redemptive purposes. The nations may be closer than you think. Explore more content from  Radical .

fetched_title: The Mercy of God in the Movement of the Peoples - David Platt Messages

title: How Do I Find God’s Will for My Life?
description: Christians use many different strategies to find an answer to that all-important question, “What is God’s will for my life?” But what if God’s will isn’t lost? And what if He actually works in us so that we might walk in His will? David Platt encourages us to align our lives with God’s larger purposes in the world in this sermon from Acts 16. Explore more content from  Radical .

fetched_title: How Do I Find God’s Will for My Life? - David Platt Messages

title: Proclaiming Jesus for the Joy of All People
description: The claim that Jesus is the only Savior, that anyone who doesn’t believe in Him will face God’s eternal judgment, sounds narrow-minded and arrogant to most people. But if Jesus is who He says He is, and if He has died, risen, and been raised to God’s right hand as Lord of all, then proclaiming the gospel is the most loving thing we can do. This gospel was the reason for Paul’s mission in Acts 13:13–52, and, as David Platt reminds us in this sermon, it is the very message that should define our lives and the church’s mission today. Explore more content from  Radical .

title: Behold His Jealousy
description: No one wants to be described as jealous. In fact, Scripture warns us against an ungrateful heart that longs for what God has not given us. But, according to Psalm 79, jealousy is a good thing if we’re talking about God’s jealousy. Unlike us, God is jealous for His own glory, and this is good news for His people. In this sermon, David Platt helps us see why God’s jealousy should lead the believer to greater comfort, hope, and worship. Explore more content from  Radical .

fetched_title: Behold His Jealousy  - David Platt Messages

title: Behold His Wrath
description: It’s not popular to talk about the wrath of God. Even in Christian circles, we want a God who is like us and who makes us feel good about ourselves. However, if God is holy and just––as Scripture teaches––then it is only reasonable that He would punish sin and judge those who rebel against Him. In this sermon from Psalm 78, David Platt reminds us that God’s wrath is one of His many perfections. The good news of the gospel is that God has sent His own Son to take the wrath that we deserve by dying on the cross. Explore more content from  Radical .
speaker: Platt
fetched_title: Behold His Wrath - David Platt Messages

title: Behold His Eternality
description: Our culture is obsessed with temporal things. We want instant gratification. We don’t want to be bothered with the future, much less eternity. However, as David Platt reminds us from Psalm 90, we serve a God who is eternal. His perfections––His justice, His love, His wrath, His faithfulness, His grace––had no beginning, and they will have no end. These biblical realities should help us live for that which truly matters. Sin is more serious than we ever realized, but God’s grace is greater than we ever imagined. Our God is unchanging, and this is good news for those who have trusted in His Son. Explore more content from  Radical .

fetched_title: Behold His Eternality - David Platt Messages

title: The Church that Changed the World
description: Can one local church be used for the spread of the gospel among all nations? This is precisely what God did with the church at Antioch in Acts 13:1–12. fetched_title: The Church that Changed the World - David Platt Messages

description: Many Christians in our culture enjoy the blessings of God without ever asking why they have been blessed. Could it be that God has blessed us, both spiritually and physically, for a greater purpose than our own comfort? Based on Psalm 67, David Platt helps us connect God’s blessings with His mission in the world, a theme that runs from Genesis to Revelation. Explore more content from  Radical .

fetched_title: Taking on the World - David Platt Messages

title: Behold His Glory
description: We have a dangerous tendency to treat God lightly in worship, preferring instead various activities and gimmicks that hold our attention. We should respond to God with humility, joy, gratefulness, trust, and obedience.  Explore more content from  Radical .

fetched_title: Behold His Glory - David Platt Messages

description: Churches need leaders who are faithful to the gospel, but we can’t forget who the church’s actual leader is––Jesus Christ. description: It’s easy to get so caught up in our own little worlds that we miss the urgent needs right around us, not to mention the spiritual and physical needs of billions around the world. description: It is deceptively easy for us to talk about God, sing to God, and even claim to be serving God, all while ignoring His Word. title: LIVE FROM HOUSTON | The Fear of God
description: Somewhere along the way, we became comfortable with a God we were never meant to make common.  He is loving, but He is still HOLY. He is near, but He is still WORTHY OF REVERENCE. He calls us friends, but He is still KING.  The fear of God isn’t being afraid of Him—it’s living with such an awareness of who He is that His presence changes how we live.
speaker: PAM

title: LIVE FROM NASHVILLE | The Heaviness of Holiness
description: Street Preachers is live from Nashville as we continue walking through 1 Peter 1:13–14 and wrestle with the heaviness of holiness.  Peter calls believers to prepare their minds, stay sober-minded, and refuse to be shaped by the desires that defined who they used to be. Holiness isn’t just about what we stop doing—it’s about who we’re becoming.  In a culture that tells us to follow every desire, Jesus calls us to a different way. There is a weight that comes with carrying His name, but there is also freedom in becoming more like Him.  Holiness isn’t the burden of following Jesus—it’s the evidence that He’s changing us.  Recorded live in Nashville on the Street Preachers Podcast Tour.
speaker: PAM
fetched_title: LIVE FROM NASHVILLE | The Heaviness of Holiness - Street Preachers

title: A  Word of Encouragement
description: Following Jesus was never promised to be easy—but it was promised to be worth it.  As we continue walking through 1 Peter, this episode is a word of encouragement for anyone navigating pressure, opposition, uncertainty, or weariness. Peter reminds believers scattered in hostile territory that hardship does not mean God has abandoned you, and resistance does not mean you’re on the wrong road.  Stand firm. Keep your heart anchored. Don’t allow what’s happening around you to change what God is doing within you.  You were chosen for this moment, strengthened for this season, and called to keep going.  Street Team, this one is for anybody who needed a reminder: don’t quit in the middle of what God is using to form you.
speaker: PAM
fetched_title: A  Word of Encouragement - Street Preachers

title: This Is Temporary
description: What do you do when following Jesus gets costly?  As we continue walking through 1 Peter, we’re reminded that persecution, pressure, rejection, and suffering have always been part of the story of God’s people—but they never get the final word.  Peter writes to believers who are scattered, misunderstood, and facing real opposition, yet he keeps pointing them beyond what they’re experiencing to what God has promised. The pressure may be real, but it’s temporary. The opposition may be loud, but it’s temporary. The suffering may hurt, but this is temporary.  In Episode 8, we talk about how to remain faithful when culture pushes back, why suffering doesn’t mean God has abandoned you, and how an eternal perspective changes the way you endure temporary pain.  Don’t let a temporary season make you question an eternal promise.
speaker: PAM
fetched_title: This Is Temporary - Street Preachers

title: Concerning this Salvation
description: What if the greatest threat to this generation isn’t artificial intelligence… but artificial faith?   As we continue our journey through 1 Peter, we at a pivotal text where Peter reminds us of a salvation so extraordinary that the prophets searched for it and even angels long to understand it.  In this episode, we discuss the rapid rise of AI, welcome MG The Mortgage Guy to talk about InvestFest, and wrestle with one timeless question: What matters most in a world obsessed with what’s next?  Technology may shape the future, but only the Gospel secures eternity.
speaker: PAM
fetched_title: Concerning this Salvation - Street Preachers

title: In This You Rejoice
description: Joy isn’t the absence of suffering—it’s the evidence of salvation.  In this episode of Street Preachers, we walk through 1 Peter 1:6–9 and uncover why genuine faith rejoices even in the fire. If your faith is being tested, this conversation will remind you that what God is refining today will be revealed in glory tomorrow.
speaker: PAM
fetched_title: In This You Rejoice  - Street Preachers

title: Holy or Hollow
description: What if the greatest threat to Christianity isn’t opposition—but imitation?  In this episode of Street Preachers, Tim Timberlake and Philip Anthony Mitchell continue their journey through 1 Peter by confronting one of the greatest deceptions of our generation: a Christianity that looks authentic on the outside but lacks transformation on the inside.  We’ve become experts at curating appearances while neglecting holiness. Culture celebrates image, platforms reward performance, and too often the Church has settled for a faith that’s polished but powerless.  Peter calls believers to something radically different—not a veneer of Christianity, but a life genuinely transformed by the gospel. Together, we unpack what it means to pursue true holiness in a world obsessed with appearances and why God has never been impressed by what merely looks spiritual.  If you’ve ever wondered whether your faith is being shaped more by Jesus or by culture, this conversation is for you.  The question isn’t whether your faith is visible. The question is whether it’s real.
speaker: PAM
fetched_title: Holy or Hollow - Street Preachers

title: Undefiled and Unfading
description: The world is constantly trying to define you by your past, your pain, your success, or the opinions of others. But Peter reminds us that our identity is not built on temporary things. We have been born again into a living hope and given an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading.  In this episode, we continue our journey through 1 Peter and talk about what it means to live with an identity that cannot be altered by culture and a hope that cannot be diminished by circumstances.  If you’ve ever felt misunderstood, overlooked, or tempted to find your worth in things that fade, this conversation is for you.  Our culture offers labels that change. Jesus gives an identity that remains.  “To obtain an inheritance which is imperishable and undefiled and will not fade away, reserved in heaven for you.” — 1 Peter 1:4 (NASB95)
speaker: PAM
fetched_title: Undefiled and Unfading - Street Preachers

title: Hostile Territory
description: To the Street Team, scattered across cities and nations, grace and peace be multiplied to you in Christ Jesus.  As we continue our journey through the letter of Peter, we are reminded that following Christ has never promised the applause of men. The people of God have always been strangers in the world, citizens of another Kingdom, and witnesses in places that do not always welcome the truth.  In this episode, we consider what it means to live faithfully in hostile territory.  How should believers respond when they are misunderstood, opposed, or treated as outsiders? How do we stand firm without becoming bitter? And what does it look like to represent Jesus in a culture that grows increasingly resistant to Him?  Peter reminds us that suffering for Christ is not evidence of God’s absence, but often confirmation that we belong to Him.  Though the world may reject us, we have been chosen by God.  Stand firm. Do not grow weary. Continue the work entrusted to you.  “For this finds favor, if for the sake of conscience toward God a person bears up under sorrows when suffering unjustly.” — 1 Peter 2:19 NASB95  If this conversation strengthens your faith, share it with someone else and invite them into the journey.  Grace be with you all.
speaker: PAM
fetched_title: Hostile Territory - Street Preachers

title: Chosen by God
description: As we continue our journey through 1 Peter, we explore one of the most humbling truths in Scripture: you are not an accident, and your faith is not the result of chance. Before you ever reached for God, He reached for you.  In a world that finds identity in performance and approval, Peter reminds believers that our security begins with God’s choice, God’s mercy, and God’s purpose.  If you’ve ever wrestled with your worth, questioned your place, or wondered if God sees you, this conversation is for you.  You may feel forgotten by people, but you have been chosen by God.  “According to the foreknowledge of God the Father…” — 1 Peter 1:2 NASB95
speaker: PAM
fetched_title: Chosen by God - Street Preachers

title: You Don’t Belong Here
description: 1 Peter 1:1–2  Have you ever felt like you don’t fit in? According to Peter, that feeling may not be a flaw—it may be a sign of your faith.  In this episode, Tim and Philip explore what it means to live as exiles in a world that isn’t our home. Discover why followers of Jesus should stop chasing acceptance, embrace their identity, and learn to stand firm in a culture moving the opposite direction. title: The Trouble with Memory (2 Peter 3:1-2)
description: Send us Fan Mail   Forgetting is funny until it starts erasing what you live for. We open with a few light stories about memory loss, then get uncomfortably honest: Christians can suffer from spiritual forgetfulness too, and the cost is clarity, courage, and joy. Peter refuses to shame us for it. He writes with purpose, repeating truth on purpose, to “stir up” a sincere mind and bring us back to what we already know but keep misplacing.  We trace Peter’s roadmap through 2 Peter, especially the pivot into chapter 3. He reminds us what to live for, who to watch out for, and what to look forward to, then points ahead to a breathtaking sweep of biblical prophecy from Genesis to the final renewal of creation. Along the way we linger on a word you might need more than you realize: beloved. When believers are mocked, ignored, or pressured by a shifting culture, identity slips. Peter starts by restoring it.  Then we get practical. Remembering in the Bible is not just recall, it is application, the decision to live what God says is true. We unpack “sincere” as sun-tested and “without wax,” an image of integrity that refuses hypocrisy. Finally, we talk about Bible literacy, why Scripture is a lamp in a dark place, and what a “re-Bible” revival looks like for families, churches, and anyone who wants discernment again. title: Reformation without Regeneration (2 Peter 2:20-22)
description: Send us Fan Mail   A message can quote the Bible, say “Jesus,” and still sell the same old lie: you’re in charge and God is here to help you win. We pull that thread from modern New Age spirituality and “your words create your reality” thinking all the way into church culture, where word-faith and prosperity gospel preaching often turns faith into a force and God into a cosmic vending machine. If you’ve ever wondered why certain Christian influencers sound uplifting but leave you focused on yourself, this conversation is for you.  We also wrestle with why the Bible sometimes names false teachers, and why discernment starts with one clarifying question: who is Jesus? It’s easy for religious systems to keep the name while redefining the person, and that shift changes everything about salvation, authority, and worship. Along the way we share the striking conversion story of former New Age best-selling author Doreen Virtue and the real cost of renouncing a platform built on spiritual deception.  Then we settle into 2 Peter 2:20-22, where Peter describes an apparent conversion and an abbreviated reformation. The language is graphic on purpose: the washed pig goes back to mud, the dog returns to vomit. We close with two simple protections that work in real life: daily surrender to the Lord in prayer, and daily time in the Bible for discernment in an age of growing biblical illiteracy. title: Why False Teachers are Dangerous (2 Peter 2:17-19)
description: Send us Fan Mail   A battlefield can go quiet while hidden mines keep killing, and that image gets uncomfortably close to the Christian life. We’re saved by trusting in the Lord Jesus Christ, our condemnation is gone, and our souls are secure, yet the danger doesn’t simply disappear. The pressure points shift to daily skirmishes: discouragement, distraction, compromise, and subtle temptations that can derail joy and dull worship if we stop paying attention.   From that backdrop, we open 2 Peter 2:17-19 and get very specific about the threat Peter is warning believers about: false teachers and the minefield of their influence. We talk through why their promises are empty, why their message drifts with the cultural wind like fog, and why smooth, dramatic words can feel “deep” while being hollow at the core. We also name modern examples of doctrinal confusion that undercuts the gospel, including universalism, denying the Holy Spirit’s personhood, and claims that reduce Jesus from eternally God the Son to a created being.   Then we press into the personal cost. False teaching doesn’t just misinform, it entices. It often targets people who are new to faith, offering a Christianity that keeps sin comfortable and makes freedom sound like self-indulgence. And when “freedom” becomes a slogan, it can quietly turn into bondage, the way so many addictions and cultural vices do. The anchor, again and again, is Scripture and the clarity of Christ, the One who tells the truth and actually sets people free. title: Character for Sale
description: Send us Fan Mail   How much would it take to buy you? Not in theory, but in real life when the moment is awkward, the shortcut is easy, and nobody seems to be keeping score. We start with a simple line our parents tried to teach us and we keep re-learning the hard way: character should never have a price tag. Then we tell a true-to-life story where the “deal” is almost comical: two missing bolts for eighteen cents and a gallon of stain. That’s the point. Temptation rarely announces itself as a life-altering bribe. It slides in as a small compromise that quietly trains you to negotiate your integrity.  From there we open 2 Peter 2 and follow Peter’s blazing warning about false teachers. We talk about what it means to “entice unsteady souls,” how spiritual scammers read needs, bait the hook, and offer comfort without repentance or accountability. We also dig into Peter’s phrase “hearts trained in greed,” connecting it to the habits that form a leader’s private life and public message. Greed here is bigger than money; it’s the endless hunger for more influence, more attention, more power, more applause.  Finally, we go back to the Balaam story in Numbers: a prophet for hire, a donkey that speaks, and a sobering reminder that someone can say true things and still be driven by corrupt motives. If you care about Christian discernment, church leadership integrity, and staying on the right way when the pressure hits, this one is for you. title: How to Talk to the Devil
description: Send us Fan Mail   You can feel it in the air right now: moral confusion, sexual chaos, and a growing insistence that biology, truth, and even God’s authority are up for renegotiation. We open 2 Peter 2:10–11 and take Peter at his word, because he is not only warning a rebellious culture. He is warning the church about what happens when sin gets normalized and when counterfeit leaders gain trust.  We talk frankly about sexual immorality in the text, why Peter says some stand in “especially” severe danger, and how the Bible also confronts the quieter sin of approval: applauding, enabling, endorsing, and celebrating what God forbids. That takes the conversation from private choices to public influence, from personal behavior to professors, lawmakers, media, and even church leadership that reinterprets Scripture to fit the moment.  Then we move into Peter’s longest New Testament description of false teachers: bold, willful, and shockingly irreverent. Jude’s example of Michael and Satan helps us rethink spiritual warfare with humility and biblical realism. We close with practical clarity: Satan is real, Satan is limited by God, resistance comes by drawing near to God, and true safety comes from ordering our lives by the Word of God, not treating Scripture like a buffet. title: Sanity and Security in a World Gone Crazy (Psalm 11)
description: Send us Fan Mail   A culture can call the cross “oppression” and still be haunted by the question it cannot answer: what makes a human life valuable, and who gets to decide? We start with the growing pressure to erase Christian faith from public memory and national conscience, then follow the ripple effects that show up in real life, from moral relativism to a collapsing sense of personhood and identity. When God is treated as optional, “anything is permissible” stops being a quote and starts becoming a worldview.  From there, we open Psalm 11 and sit with one of the sharpest lines in Scripture for a secular age: “If the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do?” David isn’t dealing with a minor leak in the roof. He’s facing danger, fear, and counsel that says, “Run.” We talk about why escapism feels so appealing, why it does not solve the problem, and how believers are called to engage the world as ambassadors with integrity, prayer, and truth spoken with grace.  The turning point is this: God is not unsettled. The Lord is on His throne, fully aware, fully present, and able to see in the darkest night. That reality reshapes our anxiety, our attention, and our courage. We also contrast two very different deathbed moments to show what hope looks like when the noise fades and the only question left is who you trusted. title: The Final Verdict (2 Peter 2:9-10a)
description: Send us Fan Mail   “There’s probably no God. Now stop worrying and enjoy your life.” That slogan sounds freeing until you notice the gamble hidden inside it: probably. We pull on that single word and ask what we ask in every other high-stakes part of life, from flying on a plane to trusting what we consume. If we demand solid confidence for temporary decisions, why would we settle for a shrug when the question is God, accountability, and eternity?  We then walk straight through 2 Peter 2:4-10 and land on the anchor verse, 2 Peter 2:9: the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials and keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment. Peter’s argument is not sentimental, it’s evidence-based: God has judged before, and he will judge again. That creates two categories that cut across every status symbol, just like the Titanic boards that read “known to be saved” and “known to be lost.” The question is uncomfortably personal: which column would your name be in today?  We also talk about consequences that show up before final judgment, especially in areas our culture calls “safe” and “private.” Peter’s warning about defiling passions, the removal of moral stop signs, and the real physical and emotional fallout of sin leads into a practical close for believers: prayer for leaders, pity instead of rage, purity in a defiant age, and peace rooted in a steady truth that outlasts propaganda and fear. description: Send us Fan Mail   A well-dressed stranger pulls up in an SUV, shows off his tech, counts a flock with confidence and then drives away with the wrong animal. title: Exhibit D - The Misery of Mr. and Mrs. Lot
description: Send us Fan Mail   The ground can move under you without you feeling a thing, until one day the map no longer matches reality. We start with literal continental drift and use it as a clear picture of what many of us sense right now: a moral and ethical shift that has accelerated in our lifetime, especially around sexuality, marriage, and the idea that personal feelings get the final word. While culture keeps sliding its reference points, we argue there is still solid ground to stand on: the unchanging character of God and the settled authority of Scripture.  We walk through a real-world timeline that shows how fast “acceptable” can flip into “unforgivable,” from Proposition 8 to corporate backlash to the Supreme Court’s redefinition of marriage. Then we talk about the quieter tectonic shift inside churches and denominations, and we ask the uncomfortable question: how do leaders who claim the Bible end up blessing what the Bible forbids? We lay out two common routes, saying the Bible is out of date or saying it has been misinterpreted, and we explain why both approaches eventually replace sola scriptura with social approval.  From there we turn to 2 Peter 2:7–8 and the story of Lot in Sodom. Peter’s language is blunt: Lot is righteous, yet exhausted and tormented day after day by what he sees and hears. That passage gives us timeless principles for Christian living in a rebellious culture: your surroundings do not have to rewrite your character, compromise usually erodes slowly, and the answer to sin is not clever management but confession, repentance, and strong community.  If you’re trying to navigate cultural change, biblical conviction, and faithfulness under pressure, this conversation will give you language, categories, and next steps. We walk verse by verse through Peter’s “if…then” argument and focus on Sodom and Gomorrah as a lasting memorial of what happens to the ungodly. The message doesn’t end in fear. It ends at the cross: real forgiveness, real safety, and a gratitude that lasts forever. title: Exhibit B - The Global Flood (2 Peter 2:5)
description: Send us Fan Mail   Most people don’t realize there’s a “half-life” to fame. Even the biggest athletes, actors, and leaders get swallowed by cultural forgetting faster than we expect, and the numbers are humbling. We start there, then follow the thread to a strange exception: Noah. Thousands of years later, his name still lands, and not because it’s cute or comforting, but because it’s tied to a warning the Bible refuses to let the world erase.  From 2 Peter chapter 2, we walk through Peter’s courtroom-style defense of God’s coming judgment, where the flood becomes Exhibit B. We talk about why flood accounts show up across cultures, why the Genesis text reads like a global event, and why attempts to shrink it into a regional disaster create bigger problems than they solve. We also tackle the practical objections people raise, from the ark’s size to the animals, and explain why “kind” is not the same as “species” in the argument being made.  Then we bring it home. The most haunting detail isn’t the rain, it’s the line that says the Lord shut the door. The ark becomes a picture of salvation, urgency, and trust when obedience looks ridiculous and evidence feels delayed. If you’ve ever wondered what you’re supposed to do with hard biblical claims about judgment and mercy, this is a clear, personal place to wrestle with it. title: When the Devil Joins the Church
description: Send us Fan Mail   Snake oil didn’t start as a punchline. It was once a real treatment for aching joints, until a famous salesman turned it into a traveling show and sold people a warming sensation that looked like a cure. That true story opens a sharper question we all have to face: what happens when the “product” is spiritual, the pitch is religious, and the stakes are eternal?  We connect the rise of snake oil to the Bible’s sober warnings about spiritual deception. We talk about Satan not as a cartoon villain, but as a convincing “angel of light” who loves to keep people chasing comfort without repentance. When we number our days, we prioritize what matters now—keeping vows, guarding holiness, and waking from spiritual drowsiness. title: The Crowded Life
description: Send us Fan Mail   Headlines pile up, slang turns official, and our thumbs keep scrolling while our hearts feel thin. We open with the new dictionary entries—riz, adulting, dad bod, dumb phone, brain rot, doomscrolling—not as trivia but as a mirror for our pace, our habits, and our hunger for meaning. Then we pull back the camera: two-thirds of people say they’re exhausted by the news, and it’s no surprise when misinfo travels faster than truth and notifications never sleep. Once, news was an event; now it’s a Niagara. The question is not whether we should care about the world—it’s how to care without being consumed.  That’s where Peter’s line lands with force: “May grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.” We explore what real grace means—common, saving, and the warning of cheap grace—and why multiplied grace looks like unexpected strength in hardship and steady kindness amid criticism. Peace, too, shifts from the hope of quiet circumstances to the reality of a quiet heart. Isaiah calls it a mind stayed on God; Peter roots it in growing knowledge of Christ. This isn’t about stockpiling facts but deepening fellowship with the Author through the Word He breathed. Scripture becomes the master science: it tells us what’s right, what’s not, how to get right, and how to stay right, equipping us like a well-provisioned ship for rough seas.  We end with a plan that works in real life: turn off the noise, prune the feeds, set guardrails, and trade the fire hose for a living stream. Make space to study, pray, and practice grace before the day starts speaking over you. If you’re ready to move from doomscrolling to a life carried by grace and anchored in peace, press play—and then pass the grace. title: The Real Thing
description: Send us Fan Mail   From cocaine-laced cola to modern religious deception, false advertising has always promised more than it delivers. In this fascinating exploration of 2 Peter, we discover how an 80-year-old fisherman-turned-apostle delivers his final, urgent warning to the church.  Standing in the shadow of his impending execution by Nero, Peter introduces himself as "Simeon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ." This remarkable opening reveals his spiritual journey—from brash fisherman to humble servant, from denying Christ to dying for Him. By using both his Hebrew name (Simeon) and the nickname Jesus gave him (Peter), he acknowledges the tension between his old and new natures that remained even after decades of faithful ministry.  What strikes us most is Peter's self-identification as a slave before mentioning his apostolic authority. This man who once demanded to know what reward he would receive for following Jesus now finds complete fulfillment in simply belonging to Christ. His transformation offers powerful lessons about humility, authority, and identity that directly challenge the false teachers threatening the church—those selling religious experiences that promised freedom but delivered bondage. These reminders form a powerful antidote to deception, both then and now. Like Ruth Bell Graham, whose tombstone read "End of construction. title: George Handel - A Statement of Faith in the Valley of Despair
description: Send us Fan Mail   Sacred music has carried the deepest truths of faith throughout history, often touching hearts when sermons alone cannot reach them. Martin Luther understood this profoundly when he revolutionized worship by creating hymns in the common language, attaching spiritual lyrics to familiar tunes that ordinary people could understand and sing. His strategy proved so effective that decades after his death, a frustrated priest complained, "Luther has stolen away more people with his hymns than with his sermons."  This power of music to shape faith and sustain believers through dark times finds beautiful expression in the parallel stories of Job and George Friedrich Handel. Both men, separated by millennia yet connected by faith, demonstrate how conviction shines brightest against the backdrop of despair. Handel, at 56, paralyzed on one side from a stroke, financially ruined, and deeply discouraged, found inspiration in Job's declaration from the ash heap: "For I know that my Redeemer lives, and at the last he will stand upon the earth."  This statement contains the essence of transformative faith: absolute certainty ("I know"), personal possession ("my Redeemer"), solid foundation (the living Christ), future anticipation (Christ's return), and eternal expectation (seeing God face to face). Job's testimony, delivered from the depths of suffering, became the spark that ignited Handel's creativity, leading to 22 days of nearly sleepless composition that produced "Messiah"—a work that continues to move hearts nearly three centuries later.  What statement of faith are you holding onto when everything seems lost? Join the chorus that spans millennia and declares with certainty: "I know that my Redeemer lives." Your testimony, especially in life's darkest valleys, may become the light that guides others to the same unshakeable hope. title: Corrie and Betsy ten Boom: Four Guarantees for Life
description: Send us Fan Mail   Have you ever felt like life's twists and turns make no sense? Like ancient Peruvian landscape art that appeared random from ground level but revealed beautiful animal designs when viewed from above, our lives need a higher perspective to see God's masterpiece taking shape.  This powerful message unpacks Romans 8:28 - "And we know that God causes all things to work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called according to his purpose." Far from being a spiritual platitude or quick fix for life's struggles, this verse offers four profound guarantees: the guarantee of God's Word (we can know this is true because God said it), the guarantee of God's involvement (He actively causes things to work together), the guarantee of God's control (over "all things" without exception), and the guarantee of God's design (weaving individual events into a meaningful whole).  The remarkable story of Corrie and Betsy Ten Boom illustrates these principles in action. Despite imprisonment in a Nazi concentration camp, Betsy maintained an extraordinary perspective of faith—even thanking God for the fleas infesting their barracks, which they later discovered kept guards away, allowing them to hold Bible studies undisturbed. Her famous words, "There is no pit so deep that God is not deeper still," inspired Corrie's 39-year worldwide ministry of forgiveness and reconciliation after her miraculous release.  Like a skilled shipbuilder who creates an unsinkable vessel from steel pieces that would individually sink, God is fashioning every piece of our lives—even the painful, confusing parts—into His unsinkable plan. We may not understand how certain circumstances contribute to our good now, but when we view life from heaven's perspective, we can trust the divine Artist is creating something beautiful with every hill and valley we encounter. title: William Wilberforce - Facing the Lions
description: Send us Fan Mail   The road of faith is rarely smoothed by devotion—it's often made more challenging. This profound truth emerges through the extraordinary biography of Daniel, a teenager whose life began not with celebration but abduction. Thrust into Babylon's elite university system designed to erase his identity and faith, Daniel makes a courageous decision that shapes his entire life: he refuses to compromise.  As we journey through Daniel's remarkable life, we witness his rise to become one of the three highest officials in the Persian Empire. Yet at approximately 85 years old, when most would expect him to coast through his final years, Daniel faces his greatest challenge—a politically motivated trap designed to silence his faith and end his life. The lion's den awaits.  What makes Daniel's legacy so powerful isn't just his survival of impossible circumstances, but the character he maintained throughout decades of exile. Four distinct qualities shine through his life, making him a model for Christians in public service today: a winsome personality that remained joyful despite continual adversity; comprehensive integrity that withstood the most determined investigations; spiritual consistency that refused to compromise even when facing death; and personal humility that gave God all the glory for deliverance. Whether you're a judge, teacher, homemaker, or serving in any capacity, your vocation is a sacred calling—a place to shine God's light through winsomeness, integrity, devotion, and humility. When darkness seems overwhelming, remember Daniel's example: God may not remove you from the den, but He will be with you in it. title: Johann Sebastian Bach - More than a Wish Upon a Star
description: Send us Fan Mail   What separates wishful thinking from genuine hope? While the world taps out a desperate message—"Is there any hope?"—believers possess something extraordinary: confident expectation founded on God's unshakable promises.  Biblical hope isn't crossing your fingers or wishing upon a star. It's the settled assurance that God has forgiven your past, sovereignly guides your present, and guarantees your future through Christ's return. This hope becomes visible to others, especially during life's darkest moments, prompting the questions Peter tells us to be ready for: "What gives you such confidence? How can you remain so hopeful?"  The remarkable story of Johann Sebastian Bach demonstrates how hope's influence transcends time and borders. Though dying penniless and quickly forgotten after 50 years of composing "music where God's gracious presence is at hand," Bach's gospel-infused compositions are now bringing thousands to Christ in Japan—a nation where "hope is a foreign idea" and traditional religion has lost relevance.  Bach began each manuscript with "Jesu Juva" (Jesus, help me) and ended with "SDG" (Soli Deo Gloria—to God alone be glory). He never signed his greatest works with his name, instead pointing to the true source of his hope. Though his impact took centuries to fully bloom, God's timing was perfect.  What legacy of hope are you creating with your talents, work, and daily conversations? You may never see the full harvest of your faithfulness in this lifetime, but God's purpose reaches far beyond our limited vision. Your hopeful perspective today might be the seed that bears fruit generations later.  When someone asks about the reason for your hope, be ready with this simple truth: Christianity has cornered the market on genuine, lasting hope—not wishful thinking, but confident expectation grounded in the unchanging promises of God. title: William Carey: Moving Forward While Sitting Still
description: Send us Fan Mail   William Carey's extraordinary journey from humble shoe cobbler to "Father of Modern Missions" reveals what happens when ordinary faith meets extraordinary commitment. Nicknamed "Columbus" for his childhood love of exploration, severe allergies forced young Carey to abandon dreams of outdoor adventure and settle for mending shoes in a small English village.  But his explorer's heart persisted. While working at his cobbler's bench, Carey created makeshift maps with cobbler's wax, taught himself Hebrew and Greek, and prayed for unreached people around the world. When criticized for neglecting his business to preach on weekends, he responded with words that should challenge us all: "My business is the gospel. I mend shoes to pay expenses."  In 1793, Carey proposed something revolutionary—becoming England's first Protestant missionary to India. Church leaders ridiculed him, but four businessmen promised to "hold the rope" while he descended into "the gold mine" of missionary service. For forty years, they kept that promise, supporting Carey as he transformed a nation through establishing schools, fighting injustice, creating dictionaries, and translating the Bible into 36 languages.  Yet Carey's life was marked by profound suffering. His first wife lost her mental health in India. A young son died. Then, after 19 years of labor, a catastrophic fire destroyed his printing press, consuming his translations, dictionaries, and years of irreplaceable work. Standing amid the ashes, he preached from Psalm 46:10—"Be still and know that I am God"—with the simple message that God has a right to do with us as He pleases, and our duty is to surrender to His will.  Rather than quitting, this devastation became a turning point. Support poured in from England, and Carey served 21 more years. His perspective on obstacles became his legacy: "There are grave difficulties on every hand, and more are looming ahead. Therefore, we must go forward."  What challenges are you facing today? Carey's life teaches us the paradoxical strength found in being still before God while simultaneously moving forward in faith. title: Thomas Jefferson Bowen: When Fairytales Finally Come True
description: Send us Fan Mail   Fairy tales always end with "happily ever after," but real life rarely follows that script. What happens when God allows suffering to persist without resolution? When the pain doesn't subside and the happy ending seems forever out of reach?  Through the lens of an animated movie watched with his young daughter, we're invited to consider the stark contrast between fairy tale endings and the reality of human suffering. While we love to focus on Job's restoration in chapter 42, we often gloss over his raw, unfiltered expressions of anguish across 39 chapters where he wished he had never been born. Even heroes of the faith like Moses and Elijah begged God to take their lives while Charles Spurgeon confessed to depression "so fearful" he hoped none would ever experience it.  The forgotten story of Thomas Jefferson Bowen illuminates this tension beautifully. As America's first missionary to Nigeria in 1850, Bowen created the first grammar and dictionary of the Yoruba language, helped end the slave trade, and established what would become the Nigerian Baptist Convention. Yet his legacy was almost erased from history when diseases like malaria and sleeping sickness, combined with the side effects of opium-based medication, led to his mental deterioration. He spent his final fourteen years cycling through insane asylums before dying in an unmarked grave, never knowing that his brief five years of ministry would eventually lead to 10 million Nigerian Baptists.  What sustains us when there's no resolution on this side of eternity? The Apostle Paul provides our answer, describing his lifetime of suffering as "light" and "momentary" compared to the eternal weight of glory awaiting believers. Our earthly biography is merely volume one that will transition into an eternal volume two where we truly will live happily ever after. This perspective doesn't erase our pain, but it infuses it with meaning that can carry us through our darkest days. Listen and discover how to find light in your darkest moments of suffering. title: Up Up And Away For Now
description: Send us Fan Mail   What happens when a formerly dead man shows up behind locked doors, then floats up into the sky with a promise to return? Jesus' disciples weren't expecting resurrection either, yet here they stood, receiving final instructions from their risen Lord before his dramatic ascension.  Rather than basing their confidence on miraculous experiences, Jesus anchors them to Scripture, emphasizing that everything written about him "in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms" had been fulfilled. title: A Ghost at First Glance
description: Send us Fan Mail   What would happen if Jesus suddenly appeared in your living room? Many Christians instinctively expect criticism or condemnation, imagining He would highlight our spiritual shortcomings. But the biblical account of Jesus' post-resurrection appearances reveals something radically different – a stunning demonstration of grace toward followers who had failed Him spectacularly.  The disciples weren't exactly profiles in courage. They abandoned Jesus at His crucifixion, denied knowing Him, and now huddled behind locked doors despite multiple resurrection sightings. They were convinced these reports were too good to be true – until Jesus miraculously materialized in their midst. Rather than rebuking their cowardice, His first words were "Peace to you." This wasn't just a casual greeting but a profound offer of reconciliation.  When the disciples initially mistook Him for a ghost, Jesus provided compelling evidence of His physical resurrection. "Touch me and see," He invited, showing the wounds in His hands and feet. These weren't shameful reminders but badges of honor – memorials of His victorious love. He even ate broiled fish before them, proving His body was real, not an apparition.  The story of Thomas reveals Jesus' extraordinary patience with our doubts. Missing the first appearance, Thomas demanded physical proof before believing. Instead of dismissing him, Jesus appeared again specifically to accommodate Thomas' request. "Put your finger here and see my hands... do not disbelieve, but believe." This encounter teaches us that Jesus doesn't choose disciples who never question; He chooses those willing to be taught His answers.  From these resurrection appearances emerge two profound truths. title: The Road Back to Hope
description: Send us Fan Mail   Have you ever felt like throwing in the towel on your faith? The pattern is beautiful: Jesus first opened their minds to understand Scripture, then opened their eyes to recognize him, and finally opened their mouths to proclaim the good news. He's not waiting for you to find your way back—he's already walking alongside you, ready to redirect your path through his Word. title: The Surprising Conversion of a Supreme Court Justice
description: Send us Fan Mail   A secret disciple steps from the shadows into the spotlight of history. Joseph of Arimathea, a wealthy and respected member of Israel's Supreme Court, had followed Jesus in secrecy, fearing what might happen if his faith became known. When would be the right time to declare his allegiance? The answer came at the most unexpected moment – not when Jesus performed miracles or taught with authority, but when he hung dead on a cross.  The Gospel writers paint a compelling portrait of Joseph as "good and righteous," "prominent," and "noble." He carried influence in the Sanhedrin, though he hadn't consented to their plan to execute Jesus. Like others in the Jewish ruling council who secretly believed, he struggled between conviction and courage, weighing the cost of public identification with Christ against his position, reputation, and security.  What makes Joseph's story so remarkable is the timing of his decision. When Jesus' own disciples were hiding behind locked doors "for fear of the Jews," Joseph "gathered up courage" and approached Pilate, requesting the body of Jesus for burial. This audacious act – seeking honorable burial for someone executed as a criminal – immediately exposed his faith. By Jewish law, touching a corpse made him ceremonially unclean for Passover. By Roman custom, crucifixion victims were denied burial as a final humiliation. In this one courageous act, Joseph transformed from secret disciple to public follower.  The consequences would have been swift and severe – dismissal from the Sanhedrin, exclusion from the synagogue, loss of social standing, and potential danger from those who had orchestrated Jesus' death. Yet at this crossroads, Joseph chose the path of courage over caution, providing his own family tomb for Jesus' burial and fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy that the Messiah would be "with the rich in his death."  Joseph's transformation challenges us to consider our own response to Christ. Are we shrinking into silence or stepping forward in courage? Are we more concerned with human approval than divine recognition? The cross became Joseph's defining moment – what will be yours? title: The Last Supper
description: Send us Fan Mail   In our journey through the scriptures today, we delve into the profound significance of the Lord's Supper, a divinely ordained memorial that Jesus instituted for His followers. This sacred ordinance, often referred to as Communion, is a simple yet powerful act of remembrance. Unlike grand monuments such as the Lincoln Memorial or the Washington Monument, which stand as towering testaments to historical figures, Jesus chose humble elements—a piece of bread and the juice from a crushed grape—to serve as the enduring symbols of His sacrifice.  The Lord's Supper is a call to remember Jesus, to recover from our spiritual amnesia, and to reflect on the immense cost of our freedom. The bread symbolizes His body given for us, and the juice represents His blood shed to establish a new covenant. This act of remembrance is not just a ritual; it is a profound spiritual exercise that reconnects us with the core of our faith. Every time we partake in this ordinance, we are reminded of the One who gave everything for our redemption.  Memorials have always played a significant role in human history, serving as reminders of important events and individuals. Memorial Day, for instance, was established to honor soldiers who died in the American Civil War and later expanded to include all military personnel who have served the country. Similarly, ancient cultures, like the Vikings, had their own memorial ceremonies to honor fallen warriors. These acts of remembrance are deeply ingrained in our collective consciousness.  The Lincoln Memorial, with its 29-foot-tall statue of Abraham Lincoln and inscriptions of his Gettysburg Address and inaugural addresses, serves as a powerful reminder of his legacy. The Washington Monument, with its 897 steps and various memorial stones, including one inscribed with "Laus Deo" (Praise be to God), stands as a testament to the nation's first president. These monuments are designed to be permanent, etched in stone, so that future generations can remember the sacrifices and contributions of these great leaders.  However, the most enduring memorial of all is the one instituted by Jesus during the Last Supper. As we read in Luke 22:14-23, Jesus gathered His disciples for a final meal before His crucifixion. He took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them, saying, "This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me." He then took a cup of wine and said, "This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood." These simple elements—bread and wine—carry profound spiritual significance.  Jesus' choice of these elements is deeply symbolic. The bread, representing His body, signifies the affliction and suffering He endured for our sake. The wine, symbolizing His blood, points to the new covenant that offers eternal atonement for sin. This new covenant, unlike the old one established through the blood of sacrificial animals, is based entirely on Jesus' sacrifice. It is a covenant of grace, dependent solely on Christ's finished work on the cross.  The Lord's Supper is not a re-sacrificing of Jesus, as some traditions might suggest. It is an ordinance of remembrance, a way for believers to continually recall the sacrifice that secured their redemption. By partaking in this meal, we are reminded of our union with Christ and our communion with one another. It is a time to give thanks, to reflect on the cost of our freedom, and to renew our commitment to follow Jesus.  The Lord's Supper is a divinely ordained memorial that transcends time and space. It is a simple yet profound act that calls us to remember Jesus, to reflect on His sacrifice, and to give thanks for the redemption He secured for us. As we partake in this sacred ordinance, let us do so with hearts full of gratitude, minds focused on His sacrifice, and spirits renewed in our commitment to follow Him. title: Bringing God to Life Part 2 (Titus 3:8)
description: Share a comment   “Engage in good deeds” sounds simple until you realize Paul repeats it like a drumbeat and then adds a surprising command: be careful about it. We dig into what that means and why it matters for everyday Christian living, not as performative niceness, but as the gospel made visible through action. The aim isn’t to trade doctrine for activism, it’s to let good doctrine become a life of application that benefits real people in practical ways.   We talk about the mindset shift from random acts of kindness to intentional, thoughtful service, and we break down a three-part formula that sticks: intentionality plus creativity plus initiative. That kind of person shows up early, stays late, takes the distasteful chore, and quietly makes life better for everyone around them. We also get uncomfortably practical about the local church: if any place should be overflowing with volunteers, generosity, and “ready for every good deed” energy, it’s the household of faith.   Then we widen the lens to culture and history. Christians have a track record of doing good works that are genuinely “profitable” for all people, including unbelievers, from caring for abandoned children to building early health care systems to staying with the sick during plagues. We close with stories that capture the goal: living faith so tangibly that someone looks you in the eye and asks, “Where can I get a heart like yours?” If this challenges you, share it with a friend, subscribe for more, and leave a review, then tell us what one good deed you’re going to start this week. title: Bringing God to Life Part 1 (Titus 3:8)
description: Share a comment   A gorgeous church building. Onion-shaped turrets. A familiar lobby. Then the doors open and the sanctuary is stacked floor to ceiling with chicken coops. The official tour guide smiles and says, “God is not real. Chickens are real.” That one line captures the tension so many of us feel today: the pressures of life are concrete, immediate, and loud, while faith can get pushed into the background like it’s just an idea.  We work through Titus 3:8 where Paul tells Titus to speak confidently, like a coach calling the play with no time left on the clock. We trace why the gospel is a “trustworthy statement” and revisit the core of grace: God’s kindness in Christ, salvation by faith rather than deeds, the cleansing and renewal of the Holy Spirit, and justification that cancels the charges against us. We also talk honestly about the temptation for pastors, teachers, and everyday Christians to avoid hard lines because culture feels hostile or because we want to please people.  Then Paul’s focus sharpens: this is for “those who have believed God” and that belief is personal. God isn’t watching from a distance. He is near, knowable, and involved. And that personal reality leads to a public lifestyle that is “truly beneficial” to others. We dig into why Christians don’t do good deeds to earn heaven, but because grace changes what we want, and because visible kindness gets the world’s attention in a way religious talk often doesn’t.  If you’ve been wondering how to communicate Christianity with courage and credibility, this will steady you. title: Ambushed by Goodness Part 2 (Titus 3:4–7)
description: Share a comment   Being “born again” can sound like religious slang until you slow down and ask what the Bible actually means by it. We take Titus 3 and trace three loaded words that reshape everything: regeneration, renewal, and justification. The claim is simple and disruptive: the Holy Spirit gives a full internal cleansing, Jesus Christ pays in full, and grace leaves us with nothing to boast about and everything to be grateful for.  We also tackle a common point of confusion with real pastoral clarity: where does baptism fit? We talk about why the early church treats baptism as the normal next step of obedience, and why that still does not make baptism the mechanism of salvation. When you make any ritual a requirement for being saved, you quietly add a human contribution to a rescue that Scripture describes as God’s work from start to finish.  Then we go deeper into what changes after the new birth. Regeneration is a moment, but renewal is a lifetime, including the daily battle to resist being pressed into the world’s mold and instead letting God reshape our minds through His Word. We close with a vivid picture of justification that feels like a courtroom scene: God doesn’t simply cut us a break, He credits us with Christ’s spotless record and promises us the hope of eternal life as heirs. title: Ambushed by Goodness Part 1 (Titus 3:4–7)
description: Share a comment   One surprise announcement can change everything: a stranger pays a debt you could never erase. We use that real story of six-figure student loans forgiven on the spot to open up a bigger reality the Bible calls grace. When Paul writes Titus 3:4-7, he describes people like us at our worst, then turns the entire sentence on one small word: “but.” What comes next is the heart of the gospel, the kindness of God appearing to save.  We talk about what “kindness” and “love for mankind” actually mean, including the idea of divine philanthropy. Not the celebrity kind that writes a check, but the ultimate gift of self-giving love through the incarnation, Jesus coming near rather than pitying us from far away. Along the way we challenge the stubborn myth that salvation is God helping our best effort. Titus is blunt: he saves “not on the basis of deeds,” but “according to his mercy,” leaving no room for spiritual bragging and every reason for gratitude.  Then we dig into what happens after rescue: “the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit.” We clarify why baptism is a powerful public sign but not the mechanism of salvation, and why the Spirit’s work is a deep internal cleansing, not a quick spot clean. title: Remember! Part 2 (Titus 3:3–4)
description: Share a comment   “I want that shade… and that shade… and that shade.” We start with a line that sounds funny until it exposes something deadly serious: covetousness does not just tempt us, it trains us. The more we chase, the less we’re satisfied, and what feels like freedom turns into a quiet kind of bondage. We walk through why materialism and hedonism are not side issues but symptoms of a deeper problem of the heart, where desire becomes a master and contentment starts to feel impossible.  From there, we zoom out to the culture around us. When a society loses a moral compass, it reaches for rules and bans while still struggling to answer the basic question: who gets to define right and wrong? Stories about academic cheating, shifting boundaries, and moral confusion point to a sobering reality: when we dismiss God’s authority, we don’t drift into neutrality. We drift into belligerence, and we end up tangled in contradictions we can’t solve with policy alone.  Then we take the turn Titus 3 is famous for. Right after the list of what we were, we get one of the most hopeful words in Scripture: “But.” The kindness of God appears, not to discard us, but to save us. That rescue rewires how we see other people, kills pride, and replaces it with humility, compassion, and gratitude. We close with the unforgettable Eddie Rickenbacker story, a living picture of what it looks like to spend your life saying “thank you.”  If this sparked conviction or hope, subscribe, share this with a friend, and leave a review. description: Share a comment   Kindness feels scarce right now, and it is tempting to answer sarcasm with sarcasm and insults with “just telling the truth.” We go to Titus 3 because Paul refuses to let believers drift into the mood of the age. description: Share a comment   Rome didn’t need another angry letter. It needed a different kind of person. description: Share a comment   If you have ever looked around and thought, “I can’t believe they did that,” Jesus has a way of turning the mirror back toward us. First, genuine generosity that goes beyond money and shows up in time, service, hospitality, and an open-handed attitude toward people in need. Then we hear a caution about conformity: the spiritually blind cannot lead the spiritually blind, and disciples eventually become like their teachers. title: Every Reason to Judge (Luke 6:37)
description: Share a comment   “Judge not” might be the most quoted Bible line in public arguments and one of the least understood. We trace the Bible’s own boundaries and show why Christians must be able to call sin what it is, evaluate teaching for truth or error, and practice honest self-examination. title: A Different Bill of Rights Part 2 (Luke 6:27-36)
description: Share a comment   A lot of Christians feel cornered right now, and the reflex is to fight harder for personal and religious rights. We talk about what this looks like when the pressure is real, including stories of persecuted believers and the reminder that the church has always had to live faithfully in hostile environments. Then we get painfully practical about our tone. Paul’s call to live peaceful, quiet, godly, dignified lives raises a pointed question: does our social media sound like citizens of heaven or combatants in a culture war. We wrestle with the difference between using legal rights wisely and treating them like divine guarantees, and why that shift can turn global Christians into angry nationalists.  From generosity to the Golden Rule to loving enemies, the thread is consistent: Jesus isn’t calling us to imitate humanity, but to imitate God, who is kind to the ungrateful and the evil. title: Warning Signs (Luke 6:24-26)
description: Share a comment   The most dangerous warning signs aren’t always in the sky or the headlines. Sometimes they show up as comfort, confidence, and applause. The point isn’t to stir panic, but to remember who sustains the universe, who sets the timeline, and why “God doesn’t change the brochures” when it comes to what He has promised.  Then we go back to Noah, the flood, and God’s covenant in Genesis 8 and 9. The rainbow stands as a sign of mercy, but the lesser-quoted promise is just as grounding: while the earth remains, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night will not cease. In a culture fueled by fear and control, that promise calls us to trust God’s rule over creation while still taking sin, truth, and accountability seriously. Now He turns and delivers four woes, not with hatred, but with lamenting love. description: Share a comment   Drift is terrifying precisely because it feels harmless at first. Paul’s “clanging cymbal” image becomes painfully relevant for how we talk, correct, post, and respond, especially in a culture trained toward self-promotion, envy, and keeping score. title: The Finishing Touch Part 1 (2 Peter 1:7b)
description: Share a comment   If “love” is everywhere, why does it feel so thin? Peter’s list in 2 Peter 1 stacks up virtues like knowledge, self-control, steadfastness, and godliness, then lands on love as the crown. We talk about why that matters: without agape, knowledge quietly turns into pride, virtue hardens into legalism, and perseverance becomes self-preservation.  We also slow down and compare the common Greek words for love. Storge is family affection, philia is friendship built on shared interests, and eros is sexual desire that needs commitment to avoid becoming selfish and disposable. Then we get to the surprise: the New Testament keeps choosing agape, a word the surrounding culture barely used, because it points to a supernatural, learned way of living that doesn’t rise naturally in us.  From there we step into 1 Corinthians 13 and let Paul confront us. You can be gifted, eloquent, and loaded with Bible knowledge, but without love you’re just making noise, and without love you’re nothing. That lens changes how we speak, how we serve, and even how we post online, where bragging can become “helpful content” and envy can hide behind a smile. title: Storm Clouds Part 2 (1 Samuel 19-20)
description: Share a comment   Have you ever felt like life turned against you for no good reason? You did the right thing, obeyed God, and served faithfully, only to watch storm clouds gather where the sun had just been shining. What do you do when doing right leads to being hunted?  In this episode, Stephen Davey opens 1 Samuel 19 and 20 and continues his series on the life of David. The pretense is finally over. King Saul openly orders his son and servants to kill David. Stephen walks you through the crushing losses David absorbs in rapid succession. His position, his wife, his spiritual mentor, and finally his closest friend, Jonathan. Every layer of stability is stripped away, not because David sinned, but because he stood faithfully in the will of God.  Stephen also draws in the courageous witness of Jonathan, a son who refused to imitate his father's evil, and points to David's honest cries in Psalm 59 as the very songs forged in these dark days. Alongside David's story, Stephen brings you into 2 Corinthians 4, where Paul confesses he too has been pressed, perplexed, persecuted, and knocked down, yet never crushed, driven to despair, forsaken, or destroyed. God, who raised us up, wants us to stand. And He wants us to remember how.  This message will comfort your heart when the storm refuses to lift. Desperate times have a way of redefining your sources of strength and rewriting your list of priorities. Every roof will leak except the roof of your Sovereign shelter. Look up. Look ahead. What you see now is not all there is. God will make everything right, even if He waits until glory. Until then, keep singing the song of faith that is being forged in your own hideout. title: Behaving Wisely Part 2 (1 Samuel 18:1-30)
description: Share a comment   Have you ever wondered what wisdom really looks like in the middle of ordinary life? Not the wisdom of clever answers or shrewd strategies, but the kind that shapes how you respond to praise, criticism, promotion, and setbacks. What does godly wisdom actually look like in flesh and blood?  In this episode, Stephen Davey opens 1 Samuel 18 and continues his series on the life of David. Fresh from defeating Goliath, David is suddenly a national hero. Songs are sung in his honor. Jonathan gives him his own robe and sword. Everyone loves him. But behind the celebration, King Saul begins to boil with envy. Stephen walks you through this chapter and shows how David quietly displays three defining marks of wisdom while Saul digresses into hostility and hatred.  First, walking wisely means responding to promotion with humility. David rises to command, yet he never boasts, never gloats, and never rubs his success in anyone's face. Second, walking wisely means tolerating the weaknesses of others with grace. When Saul hurls spears at him, David does not pick them up and throw them back. He offers the benefit of the doubt and refuses to join the downward spiral of hurt, hate, hostility, and harm. Third, walking wisely means surrendering to the providence of God without complaint. David is demoted, denied a promised bride, and then handed a deadly dowry, yet he keeps trusting the Lord and refuses to defend his own honor.  This message will reshape how you handle both the applause and the arrows in your own life. You do not have to answer every insult. You do not have to defend every slight. You do not have to grasp for what God has not yet given. Walk humbly. Extend grace. Trust the God who is quietly writing your story.   Support the show

title: David and the Sitting Duck Part 2 (1 Samuel 17)
description: Share a comment   Have you always heard the story of David and Goliath as a message about overcoming your personal giants? What if that popular reading actually misses the whole point of what happened in the Valley of Blood?  In this episode, Stephen Davey opens 1 Samuel 17 and walks you through one of the most familiar accounts in Scripture with fresh clarity. Israel is not just facing a military crisis. They are facing a spiritual one. The armies are paralyzed by fear because they have forgotten their God. Even King Saul, once head and shoulders above every other man in Israel, cannot answer the taunts of a nine foot nine inch Philistine warrior. Stephen carefully sets the scene, describing Goliath's armor and weapons in vivid detail, then shows how the entire conflict pivots on how the battle is being seen.  The soldiers see a giant. David sees a blasphemer. The soldiers see an insult against Israel. David sees an insult against the living God. Stephen walks you through four scenes in the chapter. The front lines, the fear, the folly of trying to fight Goliath like Goliath, and the faith of a young shepherd who trusted the Lord's power over his own strength. David refused to wear Saul's armor. He refused to fight on the world's terms. He picked up his sling and stones and stepped into the valley with one all consuming passion. The glory of the God of Israel.  This message will realign your perspective on the battles you face. Don't let your faith depend on majority opinion. Don't let your talents be depreciated by conventional wisdom. And don't let your past be diminished by spiritual dementia. Remember what God has done. Whatever slingshot He has placed in your hand, offer it back to Him. The only true Giant is God. description: Share a comment   A story you think you know can still confront you. David and Goliath gets retold as a motivational underdog win, but that version can miss the sharpest edge of 1 Samuel 17. We dig into the line that changes everything: the soldiers describe Goliath as defying Israel, while David insists Goliath is defying the armies of the living God. One group sees a giant. David sees a blasphemer. That shift reveals the real issue is not tactics or confidence, it is whether God’s honor still matters enough to shape our courage.  We also zoom out to the spiritual context behind the battlefield. Israel has drifted, leadership is compromised, and fear has become normal. The passage pushes a hard question: what is worth fighting for, and what is worth risking your life to do? title: An Unlikely King Part 2 (I Samuel 16:1-13)
description: Share a comment   A king is chosen while another king still rules, and almost nobody in the room understands what just happened. We head to Bethlehem with Samuel as God stages a decision that feels backwards to human instincts: not a warrior, not the most impressive brother, not the obvious résumé. The tension is real, too. Saul’s reign is unraveling, enemies are nearby, and a public announcement would look like treason. So the whole moment comes wrapped in the ordinary cover of a sacrifice and a meal, with a quiet conversation between God and his prophet guiding every step.   We watch Samuel do what we still do today: reach for the “tallest Eliab” because he looks like leadership. Then God drops the line that flips the entire selection process on its head: people look on the outward appearance, but the Lord looks on the heart. From there we connect the text to modern appearance bias, the way image can distort hiring, promotion, and even spiritual influence. If you’ve ever felt pressured to perform a look, a vibe, or a brand, this conversation cuts through the noise.   David’s part is almost shocking in its simplicity. He’s left with the sheep, brought in late, anointed with no fanfare, and sent right back into obscurity for years. That long gap becomes the point: God manufactures a disciple over time, using rejection, repetitive work, and lonely reflection to form a leader who can bear real weight. title: One Nation Under Greed (Exodus 20:17)
description: Share a comment   Your life can feel perfectly content until one moment of comparison flips the switch: their car, their house, their promotion, their marriage, their lifestyle. We take that familiar spark of jealousy and follow it to its source, because the Bible names it with uncomfortable clarity: covetousness, a greed-shaped “passion for possessing” that pulls our attention into “I, me, mine” and quietly trains us to live for more.  We walk through the Tenth Commandment in Exodus 20 and show why “You shall not covet” is not mainly about what your hands do, but what your heart rehearses in secret. From there, we move into Luke 12 where Jesus warns us to be on guard against every form of greed and tells the parable of the rich fool. The problem is not that the man has wealth; it is that he forgets his neighbor, ignores his mortality, and lives as if God is not part of the equation. The result is a life stocked with goods but starved of meaning.  Then we connect the dots people often miss: anxiety and worry can be downstream of materialism. Jesus’ words about ravens and lilies become a diagnostic test for our priorities. What matters more to us right now, getting more financially or growing spiritually? What concerns us most, having money we can manage or having God manage us? title: Cosmetics for the Tongue! (Exodus 20:16)
description: Share a comment   We’ve all done it: we walk into prayer or worship with our hands metaphorically behind our backs, clinging to something we refuse to surrender. That’s not just a private struggle, it’s a truth problem and Scripture treats it with surprising seriousness. When we “regard iniquity” and keep pretending, God isn’t impressed by the performance. He waits for repentance and real honesty.  From there we open Exodus 20:16, “You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor,” and we push it past the courtroom into everyday life. We talk about the regulation of speech in the Bible, why Leviticus links this command to slander, and how the tongue can mend a marriage or tear it apart. We also name nine common “lies of the tongue,” including lies told from fear, for profit, through silence, by exaggeration, and the most dangerous kind: lying to God while acting spiritual.  We also dig into why lies do so much damage: they expose hypocrisy (James), they fracture friendships (Proverbs), they block unity in the church (Colossians), and they invite God’s wrath. Then we turn practical with “cosmetics for the tongue” and everyday phrases that carry grace: “please,” “thank you,” “I appreciate you,” “I’m sorry,” “I forgive you,” and “I’m praying for you,” spoken with sincerity and love.  If you care about biblical truth, Christian communication, healthy relationships, and a church culture with real unity, this one is for you. title: A Thief in the Light (Exodus 20:15)
description: Share a comment   The eighth commandment sounds like it belongs in a courtroom, but Scripture aims it straight at the heart. We start with the chilling honesty of Acts 5, where Ananias and Sapphira try to look generous while hiding the truth, and the whole church feels the fallout. That scene sets the tone for a bigger question we all have to face: can we look like people of light while practicing hidden forms of stealing?   From Exodus 20:15 we track three Bible categories that expand “theft” far beyond cash. We talk about deceit as misrepresentation for unjust gain, how Romans 1 treats deception as a symptom of a God-rejecting culture, and why the church can’t afford to normalize it. Then we turn to false teaching, using 2 Corinthians 11 and Jeremiah 23 to sharpen discernment: when someone claims “God told me” while sidestepping the Word of God, they’re not offering extra insight, they’re stealing authority and attention that belong to the Lord. We also confront self-deception from James 1, where hearing without obeying becomes a quiet way to rob ourselves of integrity and growth.   The conversation gets uncomfortably practical with “defrauding” in daily relationships: wages owed for honest work, care owed to parents, intimacy owed within marriage, and even the way believers handle disputes. We close by naming theft that hides in plain sight, stealing worship from God, time from our families, and spiritual gifts from our church community, and we end with Ephesians 4’s simple reset: stop stealing, work honestly, and learn to share.
